pairs.rationale: Both call for imitation of Paul's example. Corinthians qualifies his example by his imitation of Christ; Philippians asks the recipients to join in imitating him and observe people who follow the stated pattern.

Both urge or commend holding fast to handed-on traditions. Corinthians commends the recipients for preserving what Paul handed over; Thessalonians commands standing firm in traditions taught by spoken word or letter.

The earlier conclusion says the recipients belong to Christ and Christ belongs to God. The head sequence likewise culminates in God as Christ's head. This compares the letter's expressed Christ-God ordering without making the earlier possession language a complete explanation of headship.

The rule about a man praying or prophesying with a covered head is followed by the explicit statement that a man ought not cover his head. The later verse gives Paul's image-and-glory rationale for the practice under discussion.

The statement about a woman praying or prophesying uncovered corresponds to the later question whether it is fitting for a woman to pray to God uncovered. This links the stated practice with Paul's appeal to the recipients' judgment.

The preceding verse equates the uncovered head with being shaved; the present conditional develops that comparison through cutting or shaving the hair and then tells the woman to cover herself. It is one explicit argument rather than independent testimony about another custom.

The image-of-God clause recalls humanity's creation according to God's image. Genesis explicitly names male and female, while Corinthians distinguishes the man's and woman's glory in its covering argument; the Genesis unit is not a verbatim statement of all Paul's distinctions.

The woman-from-man assertion corresponds to the creation narrative in which God makes the woman from what He took from the man and the man declares her bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh. The link concerns the narrated origin, not every later social implication.

Paul's woman-for-man creation argument relates to God's declaration that the man should not be alone and the making of a helper for him. Genesis supplies that creation purpose; it does not itself state Paul's whole covering instruction.

Corinthians states that in the Lord neither woman nor man is without the other; Galatians says male and female are one in Christ Jesus. Both qualify gender distinctions by relation to Christ, without supplying identical arguments about roles.

Paul's concluding all-things-from-God statement corresponds to the Areopagus speech's God who gives everyone life, breath and all things. Acts does not repeat the particular woman-from-man/man-through-woman contrast.

The fittingness question about a woman's uncovered prayer returns to the earlier statement that an uncovered head dishonors her head while praying or prophesying. These are two stages of the same expressed covering argument.

Paul contrasts long hair as dishonor for a man with long hair as glory for a woman and the hair's covering function. The adjacent contrast is retained without importing a separate explanation of nature or another community's practice.

The woman's long hair as glory is explicitly contrasted with the preceding man's long hair as dishonor. The comparison preserves the different judgments and does not equate the hair statement with every detail of the earlier covering instruction.

Both passages appeal to practice across the Churches. The earlier statement says Paul orders a pattern in all Churches; here he denies that he and the Churches of God have such a custom. This compares that appeal without deciding from the cross-reference alone what such a custom denotes.

Paul's refusal to praise their gathering is repeated after the account of shaming those who have nothing. The later refusal specifies a concrete reason why gathering is for the worse rather than the better.

The letter earlier reports quarrels and urges the absence of divisions; this passage again reports divisions when they assemble as a Church. The recurrence does not identify the supper divisions with any particular named faction in the earlier report.

Both describe conflict exposing people's standing. Corinthians says factions make the approved evident; John says the departure of some made manifest that not all were of us. Departure and factions are different situations, and Paul is not thereby approving division.

The following for-clause explains why their gathering is not eating the Lord's supper: each takes his own supper, leaving one hungry and another drunk. It is the text's stated explanation rather than an imported reconstruction of the meal.

The later instruction to wait for one another when gathering to eat addresses the earlier each-person's-own-supper behavior and unequal hunger and drunkenness. The link follows the explicit problem and correction within the paragraph.

Both challenge a community's dishonoring of poor people in its gathering. Corinthians condemns shaming those who have nothing in the meal; James describes preferential seating for a richly clothed person and dishonoring the poor. The occasions and specific behaviors differ.

Paul's handed-on account begins with Jesus taking bread; Luke narrates Jesus taking bread, thanking God and giving it. Paul's claim to have received the tradition from the Lord and his reference to the night of being handed over are not supplied by this single Luke unit.

Both connect the broken bread with Jesus' body for the recipients and the remembrance instruction. Paul says which is for you; Luke says given for you. Neither difference is silently replaced with a broken-body clause absent from the actual Corinthians wording.

Both place the cup after supper and identify it with the new covenant in Jesus' blood. Corinthians includes the repeated remembrance instruction; Luke's actual unit adds the blood being poured out for the recipients. The actual wording and quotation continuation remain distinct.

Both place the supper within a future horizon. Paul says eating and drinking proclaim the Lord's death until He comes; Jesus in Matthew looks to drinking the vine's fruit new with the disciples in His Father's kingdom. The two temporal sayings are compared without making them identical instructions.

Both warn of accountability in relation to Christ and covenantal blood. Corinthians speaks of unworthy eating or drinking and answerability for the Lord's body and blood; Hebrews describes trampling the Son and treating the covenant blood as common. These are not declared the same offense.

Both command self-examination. Here the examination precedes eating the bread and drinking the cup; the later letter asks the recipients to test whether they are in the faith and whether Jesus Christ is in them. The purposes remain distinct.

Failure to discern the body brings judgment in the meal warning; the later conditional says discerning ourselves would avert being judged. The repeated discernment/judgment logic is explicit, without making the two objects of discernment identical.

The account of weakness, illness and many being asleep is followed by the explanation of the Lord's judgment as discipline so that we are not condemned with the world. This relates the stated cases within this passage and is not a rule assigning every illness to the same cause.

The earlier instruction to examine oneself before eating and drinking corresponds to the later statement about discerning ourselves rather than being judged. Both belong to the same corrective instruction about the meal.

Both distinguish the Lord's discipline from rejection: Corinthians names discipline so that we are not condemned with the world; Hebrews describes discipline of loved children and its benefit of sharing God's holiness. Hebrews does not identify the particular Corinthian illnesses.

Waiting for one another when gathering to eat contrasts with each taking his own supper beforehand, with one hungry and another drunk. This is the expressed communal correction rather than a claim about a second meal episode.

The instruction that a hungry person eat at home answers the earlier question whether they have houses for eating and drinking. The command aims to prevent gathering for judgment; the cross-reference does not specify the remaining matters Paul will arrange on arrival.

The introduction concerning spiritual things leads to the later instruction to pursue love and desire spiritual things, especially prophecy. This identifies the same subject across the discussion without treating the later target as newly reviewed source material.

Paul recalls the recipients' former attachment to mute idols. The Psalm describes idols with mouths that do not speak. The shared point is the idols' inability to speak, not an identification of the Corinthians' particular former idols or circumstances.

Both foreground the confession Jesus is Lord. Corinthians contrasts Spirit-enabled confession with calling Jesus accursed; Romans joins the mouth's confession with the heart's belief in God's raising Him from the dead. Romans does not repeat the explicit Spirit test.

Both describe gifts that differ among believers. Corinthians stresses the same Spirit amid varied gifts; Romans speaks of differing gifts according to the grace given and begins with prophecy. Their stated grounds and examples are preserved.

Varieties of service under the same Lord correspond to the various people Christ gives for equipping the saints for ministry and building His body. Ephesians lists particular roles, while this Corinthians unit states the shared Lord behind varied service.

Both identify God as the one working in believers. Corinthians says the same God works all things in everyone amid varied works; Philippians says God works willing and working in the recipients for His good pleasure. The scopes are stated without equating every work with a particular gift.

The manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for common benefit; Peter likewise tells each recipient of a gift to serve others as a steward of God's varied grace. The shared emphasis is gifts directed toward others' benefit.

The earlier discussion connects the Spirit from God with knowing God's gifts and speech taught by the Spirit rather than human wisdom. Here words of wisdom and knowledge are distributed through the same Spirit. The earlier paragraph is not a complete definition of each named gift.

Faith appears among the Spirit-given gifts here; the later hypothetical names all faith sufficient to move mountains while insisting on love. This links the expressed faith theme without claiming that the later unit also lists gifts of healing.

The later assembly instructions address tongues with interpretation and prophets whose speech others discern. They develop several gifts named here without repeating every item in this list or equating discernment with an unrestricted approval of every message.

Both relate varied spiritual distributions to divine will. Corinthians explicitly makes the one Spirit the distributor as He wills; Hebrews describes God bearing witness through signs, acts of power and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to His will. The grammatical formulations are preserved.

Both use one body with many members to describe believers' unity in Christ while retaining the members' diversity. Corinthians develops the physical-body analogy; Romans adds that the members do not all have the same function and belong individually to one another.

Both connect baptism or incorporation into Christ with unity across Jew/Greek and slave/free distinctions. Corinthians names baptism in one Spirit into one body and drinking one Spirit; Galatians names being clothed with Christ and also includes male/female. The formulations are not interchangeable.

The many-member body assertion corresponds to Romans's one body with many members that do not all have the same function. Both preserve plurality rather than reducing the body to a single undifferentiated part.

The foot's claim not to belong because it is not a hand is answered within the same argument by God's placing each member as He wished. The link connects the imagined self-exclusion with the stated basis of belonging and arrangement.

The ear's imagined exclusion because it is not an eye is followed by the whole-eye question about the loss of hearing. These are linked illustrations of why a different bodily function does not remove membership.
The imagined all-eye or all-hearing body demonstrates the need for different functions. Romans states the corresponding point directly: the many bodily members do not all have the same function.

God's placing the members in the body corresponds to God's appointing varied people and gifts in the Church later in the paragraph. This relates the explicit body arrangement to its community application without identifying an anatomical part with a particular office.

The question where the body would be if all were one member recalls the earlier assertion that the body is not one member but many. The counterfactual and assertion make the same particular point about essential plurality.
The many-members/one-body conclusion corresponds to the many being one body in Christ and individually members of one another. Both retain personal plurality within the shared body.

The eye and head cannot dismiss the hand and feet as unnecessary; Ephesians describes the body's growth through supporting joints and each individual part's work. Both portray interdependence, without identifying the argumentative head in Corinthians with Ephesians's Christology by anatomy alone.

The apparently weaker members being necessary corresponds to the earlier statement that God chose the world's weak things to shame the strong. The shared reversal challenges judgments based on apparent strength, while the earlier text is not an anatomical explanation.

Corinthians describes giving greater honor and covering to bodily parts considered less honorable. James criticizes honoring the finely clothed while humiliating the poorly clothed. This compares responses to perceived honor and outward covering without identifying particular anatomical parts with economic groups.

God's giving greater honor to a bodily part that lacked it corresponds to His choosing the lowly and despised rather than enabling human boasting. The comparison concerns God's reversal of perceived status in two different images.

Both oppose division within the community. The opening appeal asks for no divisions and shared mind and judgment; the body argument seeks no division and the same care for one another. The later image develops the earlier communal aim.

Shared suffering and rejoicing among bodily members corresponds to rejoicing with those who rejoice and weeping with those who weep. Romans gives the communal response as direct instruction; Corinthians expresses it through the body image.

Corinthians explicitly calls the recipients Christ's body with individual membership; Ephesians names the Church as His body and Christ as head. This connects the expressed community-body descriptions without replacing their different emphases.

Both list apostles, prophets and teachers among divine gifts or appointments for the community. Corinthians makes God the appointer and also lists acts of power, healings, helps, guidance and tongues; Ephesians speaks of Christ's giving and includes evangelists and shepherds. The lists and order are not made identical.

The questions whether all are apostles, prophets, teachers or performers of acts of power recall the immediately named varied appointments. Their place in the diversity argument is retained without turning every appointment into a universal role.

The questions about universal healing gifts, tongues and interpretation refer back to these separately distributed gifts in the earlier list. The comparison preserves the distinction of gifts rather than assuming every member has all of them.

The call to desire greater gifts and the promised incomparable way lead through the love discussion to pursuing love and desiring spiritual things, especially prophecy. This traces the letter's own progression without making the greater-gifts phrase an exhaustive ranking by itself.

Speech without love is compared with resounding metal; later, indistinct instrumental sounds and unintelligible speech illustrate failure to communicate. Both use unhelpful sound analogies, but lack of love and lack of intelligibility are different defects, and angelic speech is not independently established by the hypothetical.

Both describe faith in terms of moving a mountain. Jesus connects mustard-seed faith with that possibility; Paul makes the all-faith mountain-moving claim hypothetical and says it leaves him nothing without love. The target does not itself state that qualification.

Both deny that an impressive outward religious act automatically secures its desired benefit. Paul describes giving all possessions as food and surrendering his body so that he may boast, yet gaining nothing without love; Jesus warns against doing righteousness and alms for human recognition. Paul says boast, not burn.

Corinthians describes love as patient and kind; Galatians includes love, patience and kindness in the Spirit's fruit. These shared qualities link the descriptions without making the whole lists identical or turning gifts and fruit into the same category.

Love's not seeking its own interests corresponds to the instruction that no one seek his own interest but the other's. The earlier instruction appears in the food-and-conscience discussion; the present love description also includes other qualities not restated there.

Love rejoices with the truth rather than in unrighteousness. Thessalonians describes those who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in unrighteousness. The paired truth/unrighteousness contrast is specific, though the grammatical subjects and judgment setting differ.

Love bears all things; Paul earlier says we bear everything rather than obstruct Christ's gospel by exercising a right. The concrete apostolic example shares the bearing language without exhausting love's additional believing, hoping and enduring descriptions.

Love's never falling and its contrast with temporary gifts correspond to the conclusion that faith, hope and love remain, with love greatest. The link follows the text's enduring-love emphasis without imposing an unprinted timetable for gifts.

Knowing in part is repeated in the mirror/face-to-face comparison, which contrasts present partial knowledge with future full knowledge. The later unit elaborates the stated limit without defining the partial as a defective or false revelation.

The coming of what is complete and ending of the partial correspond to the later now/then contrast in seeing and knowing. The later comparison helps describe the contrast; neither target nor source here identifies the complete with a particular canon-completion date.

The child-to-man illustration contrasts former ways of speaking, thinking and reasoning with maturity. The later exhortation tells the community to be mature in thinking while being infants in evil. Both use maturity language, with an autobiographical illustration in one and a command in the other.

Paul contrasts seeing through a mirror as in a riddle with seeing face to face and contrasts partial with full knowing. Numbers describes God speaking mouth to mouth with Moses, in visible appearance rather than riddles, and Moses seeing the Lord's glory. This is a related contrast, not a verbatim quotation or an equation of their entire prophetic statuses.

Both join faith, love and hope. Thessalonians recalls faith's work, love's labor and hope's endurance in the Lord Jesus Christ; Corinthians says the three remain and explicitly makes love greatest. The target does not supply that ranking.

deferred.reason: The authority-on-her-head statement because of the angels has no sufficiently specific independently read parallel that explains that rationale. The text is preserved without supplying an unprinted word symbol, identifying the angels, or resolving the interpretation through a generic angel reference.
